text:
Letter dated June 30, 1972, from the Director, Intergovernmental Planning,

Minnesota State Planning Agency, with appended comment by the State

Department of Agriculture.
Comment: The Department of Agriculture concurs in the action with

the reservation that perpetuating endangered species may be interfering with

the natural process of evolution.
Response: Although this question is academic, we would like to respond briefly. One may argue whether or not man is a part of the natural processes of change in plant and animal associations, but certainly man is responsible in both a direct and indirect way for a significant part of all changes that take place on the earth. There is ample evidence that species are becoming depleted and are disappearing as a result of those man-made changes. At the same time, forces of evolution even beyond the influence of man are still at work. Just where one leaves off and the other begins is frequently difficult to separate. We recognize that in spite of our best efforts and with the help of strong legislation, we will not save all species. Probably our best efforts in many cases will be to extend the survival of some species a matter of 100 years so they may benefit our grandchildren or their children. There is little likelihood that our most successful efforts will allay any larger effects of evolution any more than man's presence has extended it.
